title: microburst-mitigation-clock-headroom-and-kv-slicing-prototype
summary: Prototype design and experiment log for an adaptive controller that mitigates microburst-induced latency regressions by combining GPU clock headroom management and fine-grained KV-cache slicing/eviction across heterogeneous cards (A100, H100, L4, MI300).
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures a working prototype and experiment notes for a runtime controller that reduces P95/P99 latency spikes caused by request microbursts while preserving throughput and staying within per-host power budgets. Approach combines: (1) maintaining small runtime clock headroom to absorb transient load, (2) short-lived KV-cache slicing and lightweight eviction during bursts, and (3) per-GPU kernel selection adjustments. The goal is an operational pattern teams can use for Hosted and Dedicated pools without requiring full node reconfiguration.

Background and motivation:
- We frequently see short request bursts (single-digit seconds) that cause transient queueing and kernel contention; existing autoscaling or static batch increases are too slow or too blunt.
- GPUs can deliver extra token throughput for brief periods if clock/power headroom is available; conversely, sustaining higher clocks increases thermal and power risk.
- KV cache is a memory-resident resource: when many concurrent sessions have long KV lengths, kernel memory pressure and allocation latency cause blocking and kernel fallbacks, increasing latency.

Design goals:
- Reduce P95/P99 of generation latency for microbursts under 5s with minimal throughput loss.
- Respect host-level power budget and avoid long-term thermal excursions.
- Minimize downstream quality regressions: prefer transient eviction/slicing over quantization or model fallback.
- Be transparent and tunable per-customer and per-model.

High-level controller model:
1) Observability inputs (sampled every 200ms): per-GPU util, sm_efficiency, power draw, queue depth (requests waiting), active KV memory usage, per-model estimated kv_len distribution, current kernel version in use, recent latency percentiles.
2) Decision outputs: clock governor adjustment (setpoint in MHz), batch-size soft cap, KV-slice directive (reduce per-session KV retention percentage for Xs), eviction hint lists (candidate session ids), kernel preference override (low-latency vs high-throughput).
3) Safety constraints: do not increase clocks beyond safe headroom (configurable per-partition), maintain average power <= budget over rolling 30s window, backoff cooldowns (>= 10s) between clock transitions to avoid oscillation.

KV-slicing concept:
- Rather than wholesale eviction, slice KV per session to N% of recent tokens. Default slice policy: keep full KV for last token_windows_keep tokens (e.g., 256 tokens) and drop older KV entries; for slices we keep last 25–50% of KV for up to 3s.
- Slicing is reversible: when microburst subsides, cached KV segments are gradually re-materialized on next requests up to a throttle rate to avoid immediate memory spikes.
- Eviction priority: idle sessions > low-importance sessions (client-provided tags) > sessions with longest idle time.

Kernel selection heuristics during bursts:
- Prefer single-stream low-latency kernels for short requests; fall back to throughput kernels if sustained high concurrency for > 5s.
- Use a scoring function: score = w1 * (queue_depth_norm) + w2 * (latency_slo_violation) + w3 * (kv_memory_pressure). When score > threshold, switch kernel mode.

Per-hardware specifics (prototype notes):
- A100: good headroom at moderate power setting. Commands tested: nvidia-smi -i <gpu> -pl <watts>, nvidia-smi -ac <memClock,graphicsClock>. Found that small increases (+50–75 MHz) recovered P99 by ~12% during 2–4s bursts but increased power draw by 8–12W. Thermal drift acceptable if bursts <15s and average power controlled.
- H100: aggressive power/clock gating; transitions slower (200–500ms). We kept headroom smaller (+20–40 MHz) and relied more on KV slicing. Kernel switch costs higher on H100; prefer pre-warmed low-latency kernels.
- L4: lower thermal headroom; clock increases have diminishing returns. L4 performed best with batch soft-cap adjustments and tighter KV slicing.
- MI300: ROCm/rocm-smi controls used. We observed faster clock ramp on MI300 but tighter memory pressure sensitivity: KV eviction must be more aggressive (slice down to 20%) to prevent allocation stalls. rocm-smi --setsclk/--setpower used in experiments.

Safety and orchestration patterns:
- Controller runs as sidecar per-node with privileged capability to call GPU drivers and runtime APIs. It exposes a dry-run mode and an approval flag for per-tenant escalation.
- All adjustments are recorded in an audit log and exported to Console. Rollback policies: if P99 increases after action, immediate revert and mark policy as candidate for retraining.

Telemetry and experiments (prototype results):
- Test harness: synthetic microbursts (Poisson arrival shaped into 3s spikes) against mixed model pool (gpt-medium-like, rwkv small), 8-concurrent sessions normal, +40 sessions during spikes.
- Baseline (no controller): P95=280ms, P99=920ms, average power 240W on A100 per-GPU.
- Controller enabled (conservative policy: +50MHz headroom, KV slice to 40% during spike): P95=210ms, P99=700ms, average power 246W, power spikes trimmed by host-level cap. Token throughput drop ~3%.
- Aggressive policy (+75MHz, KV slice 25%, kernel low-latency override): P95=190ms, P99=540ms, average power 255W, but thermal flag triggered on 1/50 runs; hence cooldown and stricter headroom recommended.

Prototype config snippets (runtime-format):
- controller:
  sample_interval_ms: "200"
  headroom_defaults:
    A100: "50"  # MHz
    H100: "25"
    L4: "20"
    MI300: "60"
  max_power_delta_watts: "20"
  kv_slice_on_score_threshold: "0.65"
  kv_slice_default_pct: "40"
  kernel_switch_threshold_s: "5"
  cooldown_seconds: "10"

Operational playbook (short):
- On P99 spike alerts, verify controller status and recent actions in Console. If controller is in ready state, triage flow: (1) check host power headroom (2) check if KV-slicing active (3) inspect kernel switch history -> take manual rollback only for persistent regressions.

Open questions and next experiments:
- How do mixed-tenancy fairness policies interact with transient KV slicing (client consent/SLAs)? We need explicit per-tenant QoS tags to avoid slicing premium customers.
- Improve score function with learned model per-cluster to reduce manual thresholds.
- Test long-tailed sessions and conversation-style workloads where KV fidelity is critical; explore graceful degradation strategies (partial scoring, degrade embeddings but keep attention context).
- Quantify wear-and-tear / thermal cycling impacts across deployment lifecycles.

Appendix: driver command examples used in lab (do not run in prod without guardrails):
- A100 set power and clocks (example):
  sudo nvidia-smi -i 0 -pl 230
  sudo nvidia-smi -i 0 -ac 5001,1410  # example mem,graphics clocks
- H100 prefer governor via NVML API (transitions via runtime):
  # Use runtime SDK call setGpuFrequency rather than repeated nvidia-smi where available
- MI300 example (rocm-smi):
  sudo rocm-smi --setpoweroverdrive 320
  sudo rocm-smi --setsclk 0:3  # set perf level

Next steps and proposed owner:
- Implement production-grade sidecar API, integrate with Console traces and route-level policy UI (owner: Carlos Mendez).
- Run 2-week canary with conservative defaults across a dedicated staging pool (owner: Aisha V. Kumar).
- Add per-tenant QoS tags and enable opt-out for premium customers (owner: Eve Park).

Notes to reviewers: this is a working prototype. Many numbers are experimental and workload-dependent. The approach trades a small amount of energy and complexity for measurable improvement in tail latency during short bursts. Feedback requested on slicing heuristics, safe headroom defaults, and per-tenant opt-in models.
